newsitem.title: DENMARK: Freight absorbs 10-12 pct of UNICEF aid spending.
newsitem.headline: Freight absorbs 10-12 pct of UNICEF aid spending.

text.p: Transport costs represented some 10 to 12 percent of the $400 million spent last year by the United Nations Children's Fund's (UNICEF) global purchasing and distribution centre in Copenhagen.

"My guess would be that we will spend maybe between $15 and $18 million on air freight (alone) in 1997," Ole Boye, shipping officer and emergency coordinator at UNICEF's supply division, told Reuters in an interview.
UNICEF shipped about 55 percent of its goods by air and the rest by sea and land, he added.
For the airlines operating into Denmark, freighting pencils and children's school books mean big business as do medical supplies and water sanitation equipment.
UNICEF shipped some 3,500 tonnes of school supplies, water sanitation equipment -- which includes drilling rigs and pipes -- and hospital equipment by air in 1996, Boye said.
Although only about one-fourth moved through the Copenhagen centre, Boye is also in charge of purchasing the air freight space for all of UNICEF's programmes.
"We still do all the global freight purchasing...it just originates elsewhere," he said.
These goods, used for UNICEF's health, education and clean water projects around the world, represent 40 percent of the total UNICEF budget, Boye said.

A global immunization programme, stipifying that all children up to the age of five should be vaccinated against the five most common child killers, makes UNICEF the world's largest purchaser of vaccines.
Besides disaster hot spots, UNICEF also uses air freight regularly, typically in shipments ranging from 100 to 500 kg.
"Very often we do air shipments, particularly to landlocked countries, not only because of the time savings and the safety, but because it's more cost-efficient," Boye said.

"If you have a small consignment to the interior of Africa, it's cheaper to air freight it directly to the destination rather than having it shipped to a seaport and having it forwarded overland to the ultimate destination," Boye said.

From its base in Copenhagen, UNICEF also monitors all the shipping activities and packagages individual items into tailor-made kits which are ready to use upon arrival. Some 80 percent of supplies are purchased in western Europe.
"So we're not really adding much extra cost by bringing them in here," Boye said.

Lately much of UNICEF's attention has been turned towards Rwanda, Burundi and Zaire, to where it has shipped some 20 full aircraft loads with 40 tonne payload capacities each in the past three months, Boye said.
Although UNICEF also supplies equipment for man-made and natural disasters, Africa is consistently the main destination for UNICEF goods.
"The bulk goes to Africa. That's also where we have the most emergency activity," Boye said. He named Kigali, Kinshasa, Kampala, and Nairobi as key destinations as well as Bangladesh and Pakistan.
UNICEF has programmes in more than 135 countries in the developing world and frequently flies goods with Air France, Lufthansa Cargo AG, Sabena and to a less extent Swissair and Singapore Airlines.
"We make frequent use of Air France with French speaking west Africa," Boye said. "The same is true for British Airways to the former British colonies."

The group flies rarely with Scandinavian airline SAS, which has its hub at Copenhagen, because the airline does not have a substantial cargo operation, nor does it fly to important UNICEF destinations, Boye said.
The Netherlands, Belgium and France have in the past donated military aircraft for air lifts, but most of the time UNICEF negotiates with airlines through a cargo agent, Boye said.
"We work with many different airlines and work with two air brokers, especially for supplies that orginate from Copenhagen," Boye said.
Only around 10 to 15 percent of the air cargo is sent on special charters and the rest on regular departures. Much of the cargo is trucked via overnight express services to other European airports.
"We use Copenhagen airport to a certain degree but it's not very much geared towards larger air shipments.
"What will normally happen if we have several tonnes in a given consignment is that we would haul it to a continental airport...and we'd lift it from there," he said.
Some airlines give special prices to the organisation because of its humanitarian work, but UNICEF is more commonly eligible for lower rates because of the sheer volume it ships.
The facilties, provided free of charge by the Danish government, also have 23,000 square metres of warehouse space where it stores goods worth $25 million.
"We have easy access to the rest of the world from here, from both sea and air," Boye said. -- Copenhagen Newsroom +45-33969650
